rule: The payment currency is the local currency of the first bank on the path (usually the ordering bank)
test: full data; local currency = modal sender currency per BIC country, inferred in-sample (holdout checks in notebook 01)
value: first path bank 93.4%; ordering bank 89.4%; receiver-only 4.2% (18.9% match the receiver currency incl. same-currency pairs); N = 10,000,000
interpretation: The bank that sends the payment debits in its home currency; FX happens later along the route

rule: Direct payments: 1 conversion if sender and receiver local currencies differ, otherwise 0
test: prediction accuracy on all Direct rows
interpretation: With only two banks, FX happens once, and only between currency areas

rule: Conversions never exceed the number of hops (participants - 1)
interpretation: Each correspondent bank can convert at most once

rule: Amounts are approximately log-normal given sender country and party types: the ln residual has near-zero skew and kurtosis and the same spread for every pair
test: skew / excess kurtosis / sd of ln residual (an approximation; not proof of the exact generating distribution)
interpretation: Consistent with payment sizes built from many multiplying factors; the exact distribution is not established

rule: Each business party (sender or receiver) multiplies the amount by e^2 = 7.4
test: ln effect within sender country, 95% cluster-bootstrap CI
interpretation: Businesses pay invoices and payroll; consumers send small personal transfers

rule: The sender's country sets the base amount; the receiver's country adds a negligible amount (extra R² below 0.01)
test: R² sender country vs extra R² of receiver country
interpretation: The sending BIC country sets the typical payment size; why (e.g. income levels) cannot be tested with the competition data

rule: Sender and receiver party types have a negligible association on all 9,992,994 normal payments (consistent with independent assignment; not proof of independent draws)
test: Cramér's V and P(receiver B) by sender type, all normal rows; chi-square p naive and clustered by sender account
value: V = 0.0010; P(receiver B) 28.84% for B vs 28.73% for C senders; p = 0.003 naive, 0.595 account-clustered
interpretation: Consistent with separate draws for who pays and who gets paid

rule: On each sender country's inferred clock, payments follow an office-hours rhythm; business and consumer timing is nearly the same
test: share 07:00-19:59 on the data-inferred local clock vs UTC; V(hour, sender type)
verdict: Strong (clock offsets inferred from the data)
interpretation: Consistent with payments entered in office hours. The clock offsets were inferred assuming a Mon-Fri week, so the pattern is partly built into them: not verified time zones

rule: Business sender accounts send more payments than consumer accounts
test: payments per (sender BIC, account) over the whole 3-month window (the ratio depends on window length: about x3.8 within 30 days)
interpretation: Consistent with companies paying many suppliers and staff (not observed directly)

rule: CEO scams only come from business senders; romance scams only from consumer senders
test: labelled anomalies by sender type (full data)
value: CEO: B 945, C 0; romance: B 0, C 2476
interpretation: Each scam targets a specific kind of victim

rule: Handout example: consonant currency codes give 3x amounts
test: ln residual difference consonant - vowel (3x would be +1.099)
interpretation: The handout example is illustrative, not a rule in this dataset

rule: Cross-border payments are smaller than domestic ones
test: raw median ratio vs within-country ln effect
value: raw x0.62; same country and party types x1.00
interpretation: Confounding: domestic payments are concentrated in sender countries with higher typical amounts; within the same country and party types the cross-border effect is negligible
